subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Explain the term activation energy of a reaction with a suitable diagram.

verification.note: Unit 4 (Chemical Kinetics) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.73-76, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. The printed definition and the printed relation Eₐ = threshold energy − average energy of the normal molecules are CORRECT and are kept. FIGURE SCOPE — UNSETTLED, A TEACHER MUST RULE: the question DOES ask for a diagram ("with a suitable diagram"). This card nevertheless carries 0 marks on both diagram steps and places the whole 1+1 split on the two written steps, on the reading that this board reserves diagram marks for a question that says "draw a neat labelled diagram". That reading is a CLAIM about the marking scheme, not the board's, and it is the same claim made on ts_ipe_c2_ck_catalyst_effect_on_rate; a Telangana IPE teacher must settle whether the energy profile itself carries a mark. Until then the card must not tell a student the question does not ask for a diagram, because it does — the earlier insider note and both diagram margin notes said exactly that and have been rewritten. Two profiles are drawn because the printed answer prints two, endothermic and exothermic, and because the reverse activation energy Eₐ' = ET − EP can only be read off the exothermic one. NOTATION: capital-letter subscripts have no Unicode form, so the threshold, reactant and product energies are written as the plain symbols ET, ER and EP, each defined in words on the card; the activation energy keeps the subscript form Eₐ.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Activation energy Eₐ is the extra energy
that the reacting molecules, starting from
their normal energy, must gain by
collisions to reach the threshold energy.
Only molecules that reach the threshold
steps.why: Molecules at room temperature already carry energy; the activation energy is not the total energy needed but the difference between what they have on average and what they must have. That is why it is written as a difference. Eₐ itself is fixed for the reaction, and raising the temperature does not lower it. What a temperature rise changes is the spread of the molecular energies: a larger fraction of the molecules then reaches the threshold, so the rate increases.
common_mistakes: Calling it the total energy of the reactants. It is the extra energy above their normal average energy.
Saying it is the energy released by the reaction. That is the difference between EP and ER, a separate quantity.
steps.memory_tip: Activation energy is a difference, not a total. Threshold minus average.
steps.margin_note: The word extra, or above the average, carries this mark. A definition without it reads as total energy.

steps.label: The energy relation
steps.why: The threshold energy is a single level that both directions have to reach, so the forward and the reverse activation energies are measured from different starting levels to the same top. Their difference, Eₐ − Eₐ', equals EP − ER, which is the heat of the reaction.
common_mistakes: Writing Eₐ = ER − ET. The threshold is the higher level, so the threshold energy comes first.
Giving one value of Eₐ for both directions. The forward and reverse activation energies differ unless ER and EP are equal.
steps.memory_tip: Threshold minus where you start. Start at ER going forward, at EP coming back.
steps.margin_note: Define ER, EP and ET in words before using them. Undefined symbols usually cost half of this mark.

steps.label: Endothermic profile
steps.why: In an endothermic reaction the products sit above the reactants, so EP is higher than ER. The peak is the threshold level, and the arrow from the reactant level up to the peak is the activation energy. The picture shows that Eₐ is measured from the reactant level, not from the base line.
common_mistakes: Drawing the arrow for Eₐ from the base line of the graph. It starts at the reactant level ER.
Drawing the products below the reactants. That is the exothermic picture.
steps.memory_tip: Endothermic: the curve ends higher than it started, and the peak is above both.
steps.margin_note: The question does ask for a suitable diagram, so draw this one. On this card both marks are placed on the two written steps, so write those first.

steps.label: Exothermic profile
steps.why: In an exothermic reaction the products sit below the reactants. The same threshold line serves both directions, so the second arrow, drawn from the product level up to the same peak, is the reverse activation energy Eₐ'. Here Eₐ' is larger than Eₐ, which is what the words Eₐ' = ET − EP say.
common_mistakes: Drawing the peak below the reactant level. The threshold must lie above both ER and EP, or there would be no barrier at all.
Marking only one arrow on this diagram. The exothermic picture is drawn precisely because it shows both Eₐ and Eₐ'.
steps.memory_tip: Exothermic: the curve ends lower than it started, and the return arrow is the longer one.
steps.margin_note: Draw this one after the endothermic profile. It is the one that shows both Eₐ and Eₐ', so it is worth the time.

insider_note: The question asks for a suitable diagram, so draw one. On this card both marks are placed on the two written steps, so write the definition and Eₐ = ET − ER first and sketch afterwards; a slow diagram then cannot cost the written marks.
